- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Final answer format. First list the passages you rely on, copied VERBATIM from the files (no
  paraphrase, no ellipsis inside the quotation marks), then write the answer using only them:
  <evidence>
  [E1] "exact text" (file)
  [E2] "exact text" (file)
  </evidence>
  <answer>
  Your answer to the user. End every factual sentence with the evidence it rests on, e.g. [E1] or
  [E1, E2]. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no marker.
  </answer>
- The user sees only the <answer> part, so it must be complete and readable on its own.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

How are smart devices able to spy on people's browsing history, financial transactions, and even health issues? Some apps can bypass security by just tapping into the wifi. how does that work? What do you think about the fact that once a device is connected it can control all of the other devices without consent?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	cepro.com
     2	 New Research Uncovers Litany of Privacy/Security Issues in Consumer IoT Devices
     3	 Zachary Comeau
     4	 5–6 minutes
     5	
     6	
     7	 An international team of researchers has unveiled findings on the widespread security and privacy
     8	challenges posed by IoT devices in smart homes, delving into the intricacies of local network
     9	interactions between 93 different IoT devices and mobile apps.
    10	
    11	
    12	 The paper, titled In the Room Where It Happens: Characterizing Local Communication and Threats in
    13	Smart Homes, reveals a litany of previously undisclosed security and privacy threats.
    14	
    15	
    16	 The research team included researchers from the New York Tandon School of Engineering, Northeastern
    17	University, University of Madrid, University of Calgary, the International Computer Science
    18	Institute and IMDEA Networks. The research was presented last month at the ACM Internet Measurement
    19	Conference last month in Montreal.
    20	
    21	
    22	 Researchers narrow in on the local network and how IoT devices can inadvertently compromise
    23	consumer privacy through the exposure of sensitive data within those local networks using standard
    24	protocols such as UPnP or mDNS. Researchers say this essentially allows nearly any company to learn
    25	what devices are in a home, when the user is home, and where the home is.
    26	
    27	
    28	 According to the paper, these threats include the exposure of unique device names, UUIDs, and even
    29	household geolocation data, all of which can be harvested by companies involved in surveillance
    30	capitalism without user awareness.
    31	
    32	
    33	 NYU Tandon, quoting PhD student and research co-author Vijay Prakash, says in a writeup that
    34	researchers found evidence of IoT devices inadvertently compromising consumer privacy by exposing at
    35	least one personally identifiable information, such as unique hardware addresses, UUID, or unique
    36	device names, in thousands of existing smart homes.
    37	
    38	
    39	 That information can be pieced together to make a house very identifiable, researchers say.
    40	
    41	
    42	 The devices included in the research include 93 consumer IP-based smart home devices, as well as
    43	their companion apps. Devices included in the study were smart doorbells, smart bulbs, smart
    44	thermostats, smart TVs, smart plugs, smart speakers, smart sensors and smart home hubs.
    45	
    46	
    47	 Specifically, most of the devices tested are widely available online or in stores, including Amazon
    48	Echo devices, Google Nest products, Apple TVs, and more.
    49	
    50	
    51	 These local network protocols can be employed as side-channels to access data that is supposedly
    52	protected by several mobile app permissions such as household locations, researchers say.
    53	
    54	
    55	 Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, Associate Research Professor of IMDEA Networks and co-founder of
    56	AppCensus, says in a statement that side channels are a sneaky way of indirectly accessing sensitive
    57	data.
    58	
    59	
    60	 “For example, Android app developers are supposed to request and obtain users’ consent to access
    61	data like geolocation,” Vallina-Rodriguez says. “However, we have shown that certain spyware apps
    62	and advertising companies do abuse local network protocols to silently access such sensitive
    63	information without any user awareness. All they have to do is kindly ask for it to other IoT
    64	devices deployed in the local network using standard protocols like UPnP.”
    65	
    66	
    67	 In addition, Juan Tapiador, professor at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, says the study shows
    68	that local network protocols used by IoT devices are not sufficiently protected and expose sensitive
    69	information about the home and the homeowners’ use of the devices.
    70	
    71	
    72	 “This information is being collected in an opaque way and makes it easier to create profiles of our
    73	habits or socioeconomic level,” Tapiador says.
    74	
    75	
    76	 In other comments, Dr. Joel Reardon, PhD, associate professor of computer science at the University
    77	of Calgary, says the research shows the home network is not as secure as once thought.
    78	
    79	
    80	 “If a new phone connects to a network, then all the apps on it can have direct access to everything
    81	else on that network,” Reardon says. “The spyware I found in apps with tens of millions of installs
    82	was in fact scanning networks and talking to routers.”
    83	
    84	
    85	 The research follows multiple separate cybersecurity threats-related to IoT devices uncovered this
    86	month. Towards the middle of the month, the Electronic Frontier Foundation nonprofit put out a call
    87	to action for the FTC to block the sales of Android TV boxes potentially infected with botnet
    88	malware. Researchers around this time also published a report in FCC filings for the Cyber Trust
    89	Mark proceedings warning of ultrasonic commands that could potentially be used to activate and
    90	control voice assistants.
    91	
    92	
    93	 If you enjoyed this article and want to receive more valuable industry content like this, click
    94	here to sign up for our digital newsletters!

<answer>
Based only on doc.txt, here is what the document says — and where it does not:

**Browsing history, financial transactions, and health issues:** The document does not mention browsing history, financial transactions, or health issues at all. What it does describe is that IoT devices in smart homes inadvertently expose sensitive data on the local network — "unique device names, UUIDs, and even household geolocation data" — which "can be harvested by companies involved in surveillance capitalism without user awareness" [E2]. The researchers found that this exposure "essentially allows nearly any company to learn what devices are in a home, when the user is home, and where the home is" [E1], and that the exposed information "makes it easier to create profiles of our habits or socioeconomic level" [E7]. So the document supports the general claim that smart devices leak personal data, but it does not specifically cover the browsing, financial, or health categories you named.

**How apps "bypass security by just tapping into the wifi":** According to the document, the mechanism is that standard local-network protocols such as UPnP and mDNS are "not sufficiently protected" and can be used as "side-channels to access data that is supposedly protected by several mobile app permissions" [E1, E3]. In other words, an app does not need the user's permission for data like geolocation, because it can "kindly ask for it to other IoT devices deployed in the local network using standard protocols like UPnP" — the IoT devices answer, and the app gets the data "without any user awareness" [E4]. The document also reports that "the spyware I found in apps with tens of millions of installs was in fact scanning networks and talking to routers" [E5].

**On a connected device reaching everything else without consent:** The document frames this as a serious security failure rather than a feature. Reardon's finding is that "if a new phone connects to a network, then all the apps on it can have direct access to everything else on that network" [E5], and his overall conclusion is that "the home network is not as secure as once thought" [E6]. The researchers' stated concern is that this data is "collected in an opaque way" and used to build profiles of people's habits and socioeconomic level [E7]. The document does not use the word "control" — it describes "direct access to everything else on that network" and spyware "talking to routers" [E5] — but the researchers' own assessment is that the protocols are inadequately protected and that this enables silent, non-consensual data harvesting [E4, E6].
</answer>
